action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation with chronic neurogenic change in cervical and lumbosacral limb muscles, fibrillation potentials in cervical and thoracic paraspinals, and fasciculations only in the tongue; reduced CMAPs with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; mildly reduced lower limb sensory amplitudes with normal upper limb sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, hemorrhage, mass or white matter lesion; subtle nonspecific corticospinal tract and motor cortex signal change is supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: L4-L5 degenerative disc disease with mild right foraminal narrowing and no root compression; mild cervical degenerative change without stenosis or cord signal change; normal thoracic cord and conus.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 920 U/L (5.3x ULN) and glucose 108 mg/dL; blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 81% predicted, SNIP 72 cmH2O and NIF -72 cmH2O are within normal limits: baseline for 3-monthly monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic variant on the ALS gene panel; a negative result does not exclude a genetic contribution.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction with metformin, amlodipine or hydrochlorothiazide; atorvastatin and riluzole can both raise transaminases; scheduled liver test monitoring with a stop threshold of ALT above 5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Atorvastatin can also raise transaminases, so liver tests are interpreted with both drugs in mind.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not stop respiratory monitoring because the baseline values are normal.
Do not refer for lumbar spine surgery on the basis of the L4-L5 degenerative changes: they do not explain the upper motor neuron signs or denervation beyond the lumbosacral roots.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive right arm weakness spreading to the left arm and both legs with upper motor neuron signs (limb hyperreflexia, a right extensor plantar response and a right Hoffman sign) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Repeat FVC and SNIP about every 3 months and ask at each review about orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness and unrefreshing sleep, referring for NIV assessment when these appear or values fall. Interpret sleep-related symptoms with his CPAP-treated obstructive sleep apnoea in mind.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Review atorvastatin with the prescriber: with CK 5.3x ULN and muscle symptoms, pause it and recheck CK in 2 to 6 weeks; a fall in CK points to a statin contribution, while the ALS diagnosis rests on the neurogenic EMG and upper motor neuron signs.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

accepted: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), limb-onset (right arm predominant)

differential.key_features: supports: asymmetric arm weakness with brisk arm reflexes and a right Hoffman sign; against: only mild cervical degenerative change without stenosis or cord signal change on MRI, and denervation in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles that a cervical lesion cannot produce.

supports: prior L4-L5 disc herniation and mild right L4-L5 foraminal narrowing on MRI; against: no root compression, bilateral leg weakness with brisk knee jerks and a right extensor plantar, and denervation in cervical and thoracic muscles.

supports: asymmetric arm-predominant weakness with fasciculations; against: upper motor neuron signs, normal motor conduction velocities and no conduction block.
supports: insidious asymmetric weakness with raised CK; against: neurogenic rather than myopathic EMG, fasciculations, upper motor neuron signs and near-normal quadriceps strength.
against: no fatigable or ocular weakness; wasting, fasciculations and EMG denervation.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: limb hyperreflexia, a right extensor plantar response and a right Hoffman sign with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles (limb-onset ALS phenotype).
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.

Mildly reduced sural responses fit a coexisting length-dependent neuropathy (he has type 2 diabetes and reduced toe vibration) and do not explain widespread motor denervation; motor conduction is normal with no conduction block.

CK 920 U/L is 5.3x ULN, higher than usual in ALS: consider a myopathic contributor clinically, including statin myopathy on atorvastatin, while the neurogenic EMG pattern with fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs argues against a primary myopathy.

FVC 81% predicted and SNIP 72 cmH2O are normal at baseline. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).
Degenerative lumbar and cervical spine changes are common at this age; they cannot explain the upper motor neuron signs or the denervation in cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CK 920 U/L is 5.3x ULN, higher than usual in ALS; statin myopathy can contribute, but the neurogenic EMG pattern, fasciculations, largely preserved sensation and upper motor neuron signs argue against a primary myopathy.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a primary or statin-induced myopathy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: There is no nerve root compression, and a lumbar lesion cannot explain the hyperreflexia, the extensor plantar response or the denervation in cervical and thoracic muscles.

findings.finding: Right first dorsal interosseous: fibrillations +2, positive sharp waves +2, fasciculation potentials with complex morphology. MUPs: large amplitude (7-9 mV), long duration, polyphasic. Reduced recruitment. Right abductor pollicis brevis: similar changes. Left FDI: fibrillations +1, fasciculations, reduced recruitment. Right cervical paraspinals C5-C7: fibrillations +1.

Right tibialis anterior: fibrillations +1, positive sharp waves +1, fasciculation potentials. Reduced recruitment. Left tibialis anterior: sparse fibrillations. Right gastrocnemius: fasciculation potentials, mildly large MUPs.
T8 paraspinals: fibrillations +1 bilaterally. Sparse fasciculations.
Tongue: fasciculation potentials only; no fibrillation potentials or positive sharp waves, motor unit potentials normal.

Median motor right: CMAP 4.2 mV (reduced), DL 3.8 ms, CV 54 m/s. Median motor left: CMAP 5.1 mV. Ulnar motor right: CMAP 3.8 mV (reduced), CV 55 m/s. Peroneal right: CMAP 2.9 mV (reduced), CV 43 m/s. No conduction block or temporal dispersion.

Median sensory: 24 uV amplitude, 58 m/s velocity, normal. Ulnar sensory: 16 uV, normal. Sural: 5 uV (mildly reduced; lower limit for age 6 uV). Superficial peroneal: 4 uV (mildly reduced; lower limit 5 uV). Sensory conduction velocities normal. The reduced lower limb sensory amplitudes may reflect a mild length-dependent sensory neuropathy; clinical correlation required.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves) and chronic reinnervation (large, long-duration, polyphasic MUPs with reduced recruitment) in cervical and lumbosacral limb muscles, with fibrillation potentials in the cervical (C5-C7) and thoracic (T8) paraspinal muscles. 2. Fasciculation potentials in the tongue without fibrillation potentials or chronic neurogenic change. 3. Reduced CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. 4. Mildly reduced sural and superficial peroneal sensory amplitudes, possibly a mild length-dependent sensory neuropathy; upper limb sensory studies normal. The motor findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells.

quantitative_data.regions_with_active_denervation: 3 regions (cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral); bulbar only fasciculations

metadata.notes: Moderate ALS with concurrent diabetes, statin use and prior lumbar disc disease creating diagnostic confusion. patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. T is a 58-year-old right-handed man who presents to neurology clinic with a 9-month history of progressive right arm weakness, which has more recently affected his left arm and both legs. He works as an electrician and first noticed difficulty lifting heavy equipment and reaching overhead approximately 9 months ago. He assumed this was work-related strain or possibly a shoulder injury, and initially delayed seeking evaluation.

Over the past 6 months, the weakness has clearly progressed. He now has difficulty with activities requiring fine motor control, including manipulating small electrical components and using screwdrivers. He has noticed wasting of the muscle at the base of his right thumb and occasional cramping in both forearms. He and his wife have both noticed visible muscle twitching in his arms, which is present at rest and not triggered by movement.

Approximately 3-4 months ago, he began noticing mild bilateral leg weakness, most pronounced when climbing stairs or rising from a squatting position. He has no difficulty with gait on flat surfaces. He denies any sensory symptoms, bladder or bowel changes, swallowing difficulties, or speech changes. He has no visual complaints.

He was evaluated by an orthopedist for shoulder pain who ordered X-rays showing mild AC joint arthropathy. His primary care physician referred him to neurology because of the leg weakness and the spread of symptoms.
